title: Naval at PandoMonthly 2012: AngelList, cheap startups, long-term relationships and the JOBS Act
summary: Naval explains how collapsing startup costs are dislocating venture, why proprietary deal flow is dead, and why compounding long-term relationships beat over-optimizing each deal. He also covers AngelList's platform strategy (never charge startups), how his team passed the JOBS Act by acting like a startup, and why networking is overrated.

principles.text: All returns in life come from compounding long-term relationships; in negotiation, leave something on the table.
principles.quote: everything you do in life uh all the returns in life come from compound interest uh it comes from the length and strength of your relationship

principles.text: Be wary of people who over-optimize the moment; they signal they are not long-term players.
principles.quote: one of the things that I'm now very wary of is people who are overoptimizing for the moment because they're signaling they're not a long-term player.

principles.text: Collapsing startup costs give one person with leverage the power to build huge businesses with little capital.
principles.quote: there's just so much embedded leverage in the system now that a single person with a lever can truly move the earth.

principles.text: Choose investors who trust and support you, not those claiming value-add; advice is cheap.
principles.quote: go for whoever trusts you, likes you and will support you over who you think is going to add value because the add value thing you can now get from many places.

principles.text: Don't network for its own sake; build something great and the network emerges.
principles.quote: Go do something great and your network will instantly emerge.

principles.text: Treat early startups as cheap experiments; if you will fail, fail fast and acknowledge reality.
principles.quote: I think it's better if you're going to fail, fail fast.
